nameStory: The 'white-marked' part of this moth's name comes from the distinctive white spots that dot the fuzzy caterpillar like tiny pearls. The 'tussock' refers to the dense tufts of hair that stick out from the caterpillar's body, resembling little brushes or tassels. These hair tufts give the larva such a distinctive appearance that early naturalists couldn't help but name the whole moth family after this feathery feature.
description: The White-marked Tussock Moth is a common New England moth whose caterpillar is far more famous than the adult. The fuzzy, colorful caterpillars are covered in dense hair tufts and bright markings, making them one of our most recognizable larvae in late summer. Adult moths are relatively small and brownish, with the females being flightless and quite different looking from the flying males. This species is extremely widespread across eastern North America and quite abundant in our region.

idTips.label: Caterpillar Hair Tufts
idTips.description: The larva has four distinctive white or pale yellow hair tufts (called tussocks) sticking straight up from its back like little bottle brushes, plus longer black hair pencils at the head and rear that wave in the breeze

idTips.label: White Spots on Caterpillar
idTips.description: Two bright white spots on the caterpillar's back near the head end, standing out clearly against the darker body - these are the 'white marks' that give the species its name

idTips.label: Caterpillar Body Color
idTips.description: The fuzzy body appears grayish-brown to yellowish with a darker stripe down the back, and the dense hair gives it a soft, almost velvet-like appearance when viewed from a distance

idTips.label: Red Spots
idTips.description: Bright coral-red or orange spots dot the caterpillar's back behind the white spots, creating a colorful pattern that's hard to miss against green leaves

idTips.label: Adult Male Moth
idTips.description: Males are small brown moths with feathery antennae and darker zigzag patterns on their wings, often attracted to lights on summer evenings

idTips.label: Flightless Females
idTips.description: Adult females are wingless, gray, and slug-like with a fuzzy body - they remain near their cocoons and rarely move far

habitat: Found wherever deciduous trees grow throughout New England, from backyard shade trees to deep forests. The caterpillars are especially common on oaks, maples, birches, and fruit trees, but will feed on dozens of different tree and shrub species. You'll spot them from sea level to mountain elevations, in city parks, suburbs, and wilderness areas alike.

seasonality.spring: Early spring may reveal overwintered egg masses as white, foamy clusters on tree bark. Young caterpillars begin emerging and feeding as leaves unfurl.
seasonality.summer: Peak caterpillar season runs from mid to late summer when the distinctive fuzzy larvae are most visible crawling on trees and sidewalks. Adult males fly at night in mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Caterpillars pupate in fall, often in bark crevices or under eaves. Wingless females emerge and lay egg masses that will overwinter.
seasonality.winter: Only egg masses are present, appearing as white foam-like clusters stuck to tree bark, fences, and building surfaces.

funFact: The female moths are completely wingless and look more like fuzzy gray spiders than moths - they're so sedentary that they often mate and lay their eggs without ever leaving the immediate area where they emerged from their cocoons, sometimes even laying eggs right on top of their old cocoon!
confusionNotes: The caterpillars are most often confused with Gypsy Moth caterpillars, but Tussock Moth larvae have those distinctive upright white hair tufts (Gypsy Moths don't) and white spots on the back. Remember: 'Tufts up, Tussock' - if the hair tufts stick straight up like brushes, it's a Tussock Moth.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their cute, fuzzy appearance, these caterpillars can cause skin irritation in sensitive people - the hairs contain chemicals that act as a defense mechanism. It's best to observe them without handling, especially since the hairs can become airborne and cause respiratory irritation in some individuals.
compareHints: The closely related Definite Tussock Moth caterpillar looks very similar but lacks the bright white spots that give the White-marked Tussock Moth its name. Instead, Definite Tussock Moths have more subdued markings and their white hair tufts may be less prominent. The white spots are really your best field mark - if you see them clearly, you're looking at a White-marked Tussock Moth.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the White-marked Tussock Moth in the same genus, the Definite Tussock Moth has sharper, more contrasted wing markings in males and tends to be slightly smaller overall.
